title: Performance Questions
text:
In elite sport, most analytical projects begin with a question from a coach, practitioner or stakeholder, raised through their day-to-day work. The aim is more than an answer: it is a change in how they do their job or how their athletes perform. Each project here shows how I take one of these questions, frame it, plan the analysis behind it and turn the result into insight that informs practice.

title: Building a player load monitoring tool
text:
The question this tool answers: is this player’s load where it should be for this point in the match week? It’s built in R, from the raw GPS and recovery files to a self-serve Shiny app, with every decision written up along the way.
Open the app View the code on GitHub
First version live The app is hosted on Posit Connect Cloud. After a quiet spell it takes about 10 seconds to wake up; the welcome page shows while it does.

title: Building a player load monitoring tool
text:
Context

The Vizathon
In March 2025, Chelsea FC’s Performance Insights team ran an open vizathon with one brief: create the most compelling physical performance interface for elite football players and their coaches. Entrants worked from a mock dataset covering load, physical development, recovery and individual priorities, and the competition drew 124 entries from 27 countries.


The data
Four files describe a single player. The values are simulated, but the structure mirrors what a club’s performance department collects. This tool uses the GPS file; the recovery file feeds a companion research question on how recovery responds to load.








File
What it holds
Coverage




GPS
Daily training and match load: distance, high-speed running, accelerations, heart rate, with each day labelled by its position in the match week
August 2022 to April 2025


Physical capability
Benchmark scores for 20 combinations of movement, quality and force expression
July 2023 to March 2025


Recovery status
Daily scores across six categories, from sleep and soreness to blood markers
July 2023 to March 2025


Individual priority areas
Three development targets agreed by the player and staff
March to May 2025





The club around the data
The physical values are simulated, but the fixtures follow Chelsea’s real calendar, and that calendar was unusually turbulent.

For load monitoring, the calendar matters as much as the numbers. A season with European football means more two-match weeks and shorter gaps to recover and build load between games; a season without it gives longer, more structured training weeks. Three coaching changes in one season would also mean three different training philosophies. Because this data is simulated I won’t read coaching effects into it, but the tool is designed so that a real dataset could be split by these periods.

title: Building a player load monitoring tool
section: What the tool needs to answer
text:
What the tool needs to answer
Staff don’t need every GPS metric every day. They need a few questions answered quickly:

Is today’s load normal for this day of the match week? Each session is compared with the player’s own norm for that match-week day, so an MD-1 is judged against other MD-1s rather than against a match.
How is the week building? Rolling load over the last 7 and 28 days shows whether the player is building, holding or dropping relative to their recent history.
What did the match ask of them? Match load set against the player’s typical full-match output, so a short appearance with a high sprint load stands out.

High-speed running above 21 km/h is the lead measure, with total distance, accelerations and decelerations, and session duration alongside.

title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text:
The question
Relegation removed the league data feed that match physical insight depended on, and the club’s legacy data ecosystem went with it. Practitioners and stakeholders still expected the same insight. How can they keep receiving match physical insight, with context, without a league data feed?

title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text:
What I did
Two sources remained: GPS data, used mainly in training, and league-wide broadcast tracking data with different speed zones. I designed two reports around what each could support:

A contextualised GPS report for player decisions, ready within 2 hours of the match finishing. A possession state model built from Opta match events splits every player’s output into in possession, out of possession and ball out of play, and into 15-minute blocks.
A broadcast tracking trend report for team-level context against the opposition and the league, used for context rather than decisions because its speed zones aren’t directly comparable.

I lined the GPS and Opta feeds up by their Unix timestamps, validated the possession tagging against match video for a sample of five matches, and automated the pipeline so the report lands on the practitioner’s computer ready for them to add their own context. I built the system in three layers, launching each only once staff trusted the one before.

title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text:
The outcome
The GPS report now arrives within 2 hours of the match finishing instead of after a 10–12 hour wait. That speed changes decisions: when a substitute who played 30 minutes shows a sprint load closer to a full 90, staff can see it before MD+1 is planned and modify the session.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Charts made in different tools drift apart. A ggplot in a report, a Shiny app and a slide deck each end up with their own colours and fonts, and colour starts to mean nothing in particular. The reader has to work out what to look at every time.
I wanted one set of rules that every output inherits automatically, so the design decisions are made once and the reader’s attention goes straight to the point.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck

Charts made in different tools drift apart. A ggplot in a report, a Shiny app and a slide deck each end up with their own colours and fonts, and colour starts to mean nothing in particular. The reader has to work out what to look at every time.
I wanted one set of rules that every output inherits automatically, so the design decisions are made once and the reader’s attention goes straight to the point.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Three words, turned into rules
The brand is built around three words: clear, analytical, sharp. Each one became a rule I could apply without thinking:

Clear: grey carries context and one colour carries the message. Every chart title states the answer, not the topic.
Analytical: colour has a job. Categorical, sequential, diverging and status colours are separate palettes, and none is borrowed for another’s purpose.
Sharp: one typeface (Inter), two weights, tabular numbers and no decoration that doesn’t carry information.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
The palette









Slate gives structure, signal teal is the single accent, and a cool grey called context is used for everything that supports the message rather than being the message. Status colours are reserved for state (in range, monitor, out of range) and always appear with an icon or a word, never colour alone.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
section: The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point
text:
The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point
The same data, drawn with default settings and then with the system. The default gives every player a different colour, so nothing stands out. With the system, the one player the chart is about is the only thing in colour, and the title says what the reader should take away.

BeforeAfter

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Style as code
The rules live in one tokens file and are packaged for each tool I use, so a chart picks up the system with a line or two:
source("R/theme_md.R")

ggplot(df, aes(session, hsr, colour = player)) +
  geom_line() +
  md_highlight("Player 3") +   # grey for everyone except the focus
  theme_md()                   # type, gridlines, titles and captions
The same values drive a matplotlib and Plotly theme for Python, a Streamlit configuration, a Quarto slide theme, a PowerPoint template and this website.


1 source of truth for every colour and type style


6 tools that inherit it: R, Python, Streamlit, Quarto, PowerPoint, web


AA WCAG contrast for all text, in light and dark mode

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
What I’d do next
Package the R theme as a small installable package with its own tests, so colleagues could adopt it with library(mdtheme) and get updates automatically.

title: About
text:
I’m a data scientist who has spent six years inside elite football, first as a performance data analyst and now leading data insight for the Sport Science and Medical departments at Leicester City Football Club. My job is to turn large, messy performance data into information that coaches, practitioners and senior staff trust and act on.
I work across the whole data lifecycle: owning pipelines from external providers, building models, and designing self-serve tools so people can answer their own questions. I care as much about how an insight is communicated as about the analysis behind it.

title: Turning complex performance data into clear decisions
text:
Michael Davies, PhD


I’m a senior data scientist with six years in elite football, currently leading data insight for the Sport Science and Medical departments at Leicester City. I build the pipelines, models and self-serve tools that inform decision-making, and I take just as much care over communicating the results, turning analysis into clear messages that stakeholders can act on. I’ve line managed students who have gone on to build their own careers in football. This year I completed my PhD on the context behind physical performance in elite men’s football. It taught me how to plan and frame a performance question: what needs to be measured, which factors contribute, and how to back the answer with mathematical rigour. I apply that same approach to everything I build.
